sections.md:
You meet central tendency every day in economic news.

- **Per capita income** = national income ÷ population. It is an arithmetic mean — so it can rise even if most people's incomes are stagnant, if the incomes at the top rise fast. Economists therefore also look at the median and at the distribution.
- **Average yield** of wheat in Punjab vs Bihar (tonnes per hectare) helps compare farm productivity.
- **Median age** of India's population (under 30 years, among the youngest of big economies) is quoted to describe the 'demographic dividend'.
- **Modal** class of land holdings — most Indian farmers hold less than one hectare — explains why small-farm policies matter.
- **Consumer price indices** are weighted averages of price changes (Chapter 7).

A thoughtful reader always asks: *which* average is this, and is it the right one for the question?

**Conclusion of the chapter.** Measures of central tendency summarise data into a single representative value. The arithmetic mean uses every value and is algebraically powerful but is pulled by extremes; the median is a positional average that resists extremes and handles open-ended classes; the mode shows the most common value and works even for attributes. Quartiles and percentiles tell relative position. The choice depends on the data and the purpose — but no single average tells everything, which is why the spread of data also matters.

story.title: Three averages at the cricket nets

parts.md: Coach Fernandes in Goa had to pick one opener from three batters for the district team. Their scores in the last seven matches: Aditi — 30, 32, 28, 35, 31, 29, 33; Rohan — 0, 2, 5, 150, 4, 3, 6; Kabir — 40, 10, 40, 12, 40, 15, 40.

He calculated means: Aditi 218/7 ≈ 31.1; Rohan 170/7 ≈ 24.3; Kabir 197/7 ≈ 28.1. Then medians: Aditi 31, Rohan 4, Kabir 40. Modes: Aditi has none, Rohan none, Kabir 40. Rohan's one big innings of 150 pulled his mean up, but his median of 4 showed he usually failed early.

Kabir's median and mode looked brilliant, but his scores swung between 10 and 40. Aditi was consistent — her mean, median and middle scores all sat near 31. Fernandes picked Aditi as opener and Kabir at number three. 'One average is a clue,' he told the team, 'three averages are a story.' In Class 11, you will learn to read that story; in higher classes, you will measure the swings too.

Verify the same mean by the step-deviation method with A = 25, c = 10.

summary: A measure of central tendency is a single value representing the whole data set.
Mean = ΣX ÷ N; discrete ΣfX ÷ Σf; grouped data use mid-points: Σfm ÷ Σf.
Short-cut and step-deviation methods give the same mean with easier arithmetic.
Σ(X − X̄) = 0; total = N × mean; combined mean = (N₁X̄₁ + N₂X̄₂) ÷ (N₁ + N₂).
Weighted mean = ΣWX ÷ ΣW, used when items differ in importance.
The mean is distorted by extreme values and cannot handle open-ended classes easily.
Median is the middle value of arranged data: (N + 1)/2th item; grouped: L + [(N/2 − c.f.)/f] × h.
Quartiles split data into four parts; percentiles into 100; they show relative position.
Mode is the most frequent value; grouped: L + [(f1 − f0)/(2f1 − f0 − f2)] × h.
Median can be found from ogives; mode from a histogram.
Symmetrical: mean = median = mode; moderately skewed: Mode ≈ 3 Median − 2 Mean.
Use the median for skewed data like incomes; the mode for most-common items; the mean for algebraic work.

glossary.d: An average based on position in an arranged series (median, quartiles).
Class with the highest frequency.
Lack of symmetry in a distribution.
Numbers showing the relative importance of items.
Quartiles, deciles and percentiles that divide data into equal parts.

rd-school-c11-economics-a.stats-ch06-cor.title: Correlation
rd-school-c11-economics-a.stats-ch06-cor.subtitle: Do two things move together? Scatter diagrams, Karl Pearson's r and Spearman's rank

sections.md:
Every May in Nagpur, ice-cream sales soar. So do cases of sunstroke. Does eating ice-cream cause sunstroke? Of course not — both rise because of a third thing, the scorching heat.

This tiny puzzle contains the whole of this chapter. Many economic variables **move together**: price and quantity demanded, income and spending, rainfall and crop yield, advertisement and sales. **Correlation** measures the **direction and intensity** of the relationship between two variables. It does **not**, by itself, prove that one causes the other.

In earlier chapters you summarised *one* variable at a time — its average, its distribution. Now you study *two* variables together, using bivariate data like the table of shops' advertising and sales you met in Chapter 3.

We will learn three tools, in the textbook's order:
1. **Scatter diagram** — a picture.
2. **Karl Pearson's coefficient of correlation (r)** — a number for measurable variables.
3. **Spearman's rank correlation (rs)** — a number when only ranks are available.

Throughout, remember the golden rule: **correlation is not causation.**

**By direction:**
- **Positive correlation** — both variables move in the **same direction**. Higher income → higher consumption; more fertiliser → more yield (up to a point). Rise together, fall together.
- **Negative correlation** — they move in **opposite directions**. Higher price → lower quantity demanded; more hours of TV → fewer hours of study.

**By intensity:** perfect, high, moderate, low, or zero (no correlation).

**By form:** **linear** (points lie close to a straight line; constant ratio of change) and **non-linear** (points follow a curve).

**Correlation vs causation.** Two variables may be correlated because:
1. One genuinely causes the other (rain and crop yield).
2. Both are affected by a **third variable** (ice-cream and sunstroke, both driven by heat).
3. Pure **chance** (spurious or nonsense correlation) — the number of films released and the number of cricket matches played in a year might be correlated by accident.

So correlation tells us *whether and how strongly* variables move together, not *why*. Economic theory, common sense and careful study must supply the 'why'.

check.q: Sales of umbrellas and sales of raincoats rise together in July. The most likely reason is:
options: Both are driven by the monsoon
check.why: Both variables respond to a common third factor, the rain, so their correlation does not imply that one causes the other.

sections.md:
A **scatter diagram** plots each pair (X, Y) as a dot on a graph. The pattern of dots shows the relationship visually:

- Dots rising from lower-left to upper-right → **positive** correlation.
- Dots falling from upper-left to lower-right → **negative** correlation.
- Dots lying exactly on a rising (or falling) straight line → **perfect** positive (or negative) correlation.
- Dots closely clustered around a line → **high** correlation; widely spread → **low**.
- Dots scattered with no pattern → **no** correlation.
- Dots following a curve → **non-linear** relationship.

**How to draw one:** choose X for the horizontal axis and Y for the vertical; pick scales so that the dots spread over most of the graph; plot each pair; do **not** join the dots.

**Merits:** simple, visual, not affected by extreme values, shows non-linear patterns too.
**Limitation:** gives no exact numerical measure — two people may judge 'high' differently. For a precise figure we need r.

check.q: In a scatter diagram, all points lie on a straight line falling from left to right. The correlation is:
check.why: Points exactly on a downward straight line show perfect negative correlation, r = −1.

sections.h: The idea behind r: products of deviations
sections.md:
Why does Pearson's formula work? Draw a vertical line at X̄ and a horizontal line at Ȳ on a scatter diagram. They divide the graph into four quadrants.

- In the **upper-right** quadrant, x = X − X̄ is positive and y = Y − Ȳ is positive, so **xy > 0**.
- In the **lower-left**, both are negative, so again **xy > 0**.
- In the **upper-left** and **lower-right**, one is positive and one negative, so **xy < 0**.

If most points fall in the upper-right and lower-left quadrants, Σxy is large and positive → positive correlation. If most fall in the other two, Σxy is negative → negative correlation. If points are spread evenly over all four, the positive and negative products cancel and Σxy ≈ 0 → no correlation.

Σxy ÷ N is called the **covariance**. But covariance depends on units (rupees × kilograms!). Dividing by the standard deviations σx and σy removes the units and squeezes the value between −1 and +1. That is r.

sections.md:
Also called the **product moment correlation coefficient**, r measures the degree of **linear** relationship between two measurable variables.

**Formula (actual mean method):**

r = Σxy ÷ √(Σx² × Σy²), where x = X − X̄ and y = Y − Ȳ.

Equivalently, r = Σxy ÷ (N σx σy), using standard deviations.

**Direct (raw data) formula:**

r = [NΣXY − ΣX ΣY] ÷ √{[NΣX² − (ΣX)²] × [NΣY² − (ΣY)²]}

**Step deviation (assumed mean) formula**, with dx = (X − A)/h and dy = (Y − B)/k:

r = [NΣdxdy − Σdx Σdy] ÷ √{[NΣdx² − (Σdx)²] × [NΣdy² − (Σdy)²]}

**Properties of r:**
1. r lies between **−1 and +1**.
2. r has no unit — it is a pure number.
3. r is **independent of change of origin and scale**: adding a constant to X, or multiplying it by a positive constant, does not change r. (This is why the step-deviation method works.)
4. r = 0 means **no linear** relationship — there may still be a non-linear one.
5. r measures only linear association, and is sensitive to extreme values.

**Interpreting r:**
| Value of r | Degree |
|---|---|
| +1 / −1 | Perfect |
| ±0.7 to ±0.99 | High |
| ±0.3 to ±0.7 | Moderate |
| ±0.01 to ±0.3 | Low |
| 0 | No linear correlation |

These cut-offs are rules of thumb, not laws; with small samples, even a fairly high r can arise by chance.

check.q: If every value of X is multiplied by 10, Karl Pearson's r between X and Y will:
check.why: r is independent of change of scale (by a positive constant) and origin, so it is unchanged.

sections.md:
Sometimes variables cannot be measured precisely but can be **ranked**: beauty, honesty, intelligence, judges' preferences in a dance contest. Or the data have extreme values that distort r. Then we use **Spearman's rank correlation coefficient**, developed by the British psychologist Charles Spearman.

**Formula (no ties):**

rs = 1 − [6ΣD²] ÷ [n(n² − 1)], or equivalently 1 − 6ΣD² ÷ (n³ − n)

where D = difference between the two ranks of each item and n = number of pairs.

**Steps:**
1. Rank X values (1 for highest or lowest — be consistent) and rank Y values.
2. Find D = R1 − R2 for each item; check ΣD = 0.
3. Square and add: ΣD².
4. Apply the formula.

The textbook treats three cases: **(a) ranks are given** (judges' rankings); **(b) ranks are not given** — you rank the actual values yourself first; **(c) ranks are repeated** (ties).

**Tied (repeated) ranks:** if two or more items have equal values, give each the **average** of the ranks they would occupy. If two items tie for 3rd and 4th place, each gets 3.5. Then a correction factor is added for each tie: ΣD² is replaced by ΣD² + Σ(m³ − m)/12, where m is the number of items in that tie.

**Properties:** rs also lies between −1 and +1. It is easy to compute and understand, works for qualitative data and is not affected by extreme values. But it loses information because it uses only ranks, not actual values, and is generally less precise than r for measurable data. When data have no ties, rs equals Pearson's r computed on the ranks themselves.

check.q: Two judges rank 5 dancers. ΣD² = 0. Spearman's rs is:
check.why: With ΣD² = 0 the formula gives 1 − 0 = 1, perfect agreement between the judges.

sections.h: Rank correlation with ties, step by step
sections.md:
Marks of five students in Economics and Statistics:

| Student | Econ | Rank R1 | Stats | Rank R2 | D | D² |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| A | 80 | 1 | 70 | 2 | −1 | 1 |
| B | 64 | 2.5 | 72 | 1 | 1.5 | 2.25 |
| C | 64 | 2.5 | 60 | 3 | −0.5 | 0.25 |
| D | 50 | 4 | 55 | 4 | 0 | 0 |
| E | 45 | 5 | 40 | 5 | 0 | 0 |

- B and C tie in Economics for ranks 2 and 3 → each gets 2.5.
- ΣD = −1 + 1.5 − 0.5 + 0 + 0 = 0 ✓.
- ΣD² = 3.5. One tie of m = 2 → correction (2³ − 2)/12 = 6/12 = 0.5. Corrected ΣD² = 4.
- rs = 1 − (6 × 4) ÷ (5 × 24) = 1 − 24/120 = **0.8**.

High positive rank correlation: students who do well in Economics tend to do well in Statistics.

check.q: Three items tie for ranks 4, 5 and 6. Each gets rank:
check.why: The average of 4, 5 and 6 is 15 ÷ 3 = 5, so each tied item is given rank 5.

sections.md:
**When to use which tool:**

| Situation | Tool |
|---|---|
| Quick visual check, spotting non-linear pattern | Scatter diagram |
| Measurable variables, linear relation | Karl Pearson's r |
| Qualitative variables, ranks, or extreme values | Spearman's rs |

**Common mistakes:**
- Treating correlation as proof of cause. A city's number of mobile towers and its number of cars may be highly correlated — both grow with population and income.
- Concluding 'no relationship' from r = 0. If Y = X² for X from −3 to +3, r = 0, but Y depends perfectly on X — the relationship is non-linear.
- Using very small samples: with 3 or 4 pairs, a high r can arise by chance.
- Mixing groups: combining data from very different regions can create or hide a correlation.

In economics, correlation helps test theories (does saving rise with income?), choose policy (is spending on schools linked with literacy?), and forecast (if two series move together, one may signal the other). The next step, **regression**, which estimates *how much* Y changes when X changes, is studied in higher classes.

**Conclusion.** Correlation studies the relationship between two variables: its direction (positive or negative), degree (from perfect to none) and form (linear or not). The scatter diagram shows it, Karl Pearson's r measures linear correlation between measurable variables, and Spearman's rs measures correlation of ranks. None of them proves causation.

> Did you know? Karl Pearson founded the world's first university statistics department, at University College London, in 1911.

check.q: For the points (−2, 4), (−1, 1), (0, 0), (1, 1), (2, 4), Karl Pearson's r is 0. This means:
options: There is no linear relationship, though a non-linear one exists
check.why: Here Y = X² exactly, a curved relationship, which r cannot detect because it measures only linear association.

parts.md: Ramesh runs a tea stall outside a college in Kochi. His daughter Nisha, studying economics, noticed that on some days he sold 300 cups and on others only 150. 'It's the weather, Achan,' she said. He laughed: 'It's the exams. When there are exams, students drink more tea.'

For 30 days Nisha recorded three things: cups sold, the day's maximum temperature, and whether it was an exam week. Her scatter diagram of cups against temperature showed dots falling from left to right — cooler, rainy days, more tea. She computed Pearson's r = −0.62, a moderate negative correlation.

Then she split the days into exam and non-exam weeks. Within each group the negative link with temperature remained, but exam days sold about 60 cups more on average. Both of them were partly right. Ramesh began keeping extra milk on cool exam days. Nisha's lesson for her project: correlation points you to a pattern, but you must think about *other* variables before deciding what causes what.

summary: Correlation measures the direction and intensity of the relationship between two variables.
Positive: same direction; negative: opposite directions; linear or non-linear in form.
Correlation does not imply causation — a third factor or chance may be at work.
A scatter diagram shows the relationship visually but gives no exact number.
Covariance is the average product of deviations; r standardises it.
Karl Pearson's r = Σxy ÷ √(Σx² Σy²) for measurable variables; direct and step-deviation forms give the same value.
r lies between −1 and +1 and has no unit.
r is independent of change of origin and scale.
r = 0 means no linear relationship; a non-linear one may still exist.
Spearman's rs = 1 − 6ΣD² ÷ n(n² − 1), used for ranks and qualitative data.

rd-school-c11-economics-a.stats-ch07-ind.title: Index Numbers
rd-school-c11-economics-a.stats-ch07-ind.subtitle: How India measures rising prices, factory output and the stock market — with one number

sections.md:
Your grandmother remembers buying a kilo of sugar for a couple of rupees. Today it costs over ₹40. Petrol, school fees, train tickets — all have risen, but by different amounts, and some prices (mobile data, for instance) have fallen. So by how much has the **cost of living** really gone up?

No single price can answer that. We need a way to combine changes in hundreds of prices into **one number**. That number is an **index number**.

An **index number** is a statistical device for measuring **relative changes** in a group of related variables over time (or across places). It is expressed as a percentage of a **base period**, whose index is set at 100. If the Consumer Price Index is 190 today with base 2012 = 100, prices on average are 90% higher than in 2012.

The textbook opens with questions like these: *How has the price of a group of goods changed? Has industrial production risen? Have workers become better or worse off?* Each needs an index. Because index numbers show the 'pressure' building in an economy — like a barometer shows air pressure — they are often called **economic barometers**.

Index numbers are everywhere in the news: CPI inflation, WPI, the Index of Industrial Production, the Sensex. This chapter shows how they are built, which ones India uses, what issues arise in building them, and how they are used.

Notation: **p0** = price in base period, **p1** = price in current period, **q0** and **q1** = quantities.

**1. Simple aggregative method**

P01 = (Σp1 ÷ Σp0) × 100

Add up current prices, add up base prices, compare. Simple, but it is distorted by units — a commodity quoted per quintal swamps one quoted per kg — and it treats all items as equally important.

**2. Simple average of price relatives**

A **price relative** = (p1 ÷ p0) × 100 for each item. Then

P01 = Σ(p1/p0 × 100) ÷ N

Because price relatives are percentages, units no longer matter. But all items still get equal importance — salt counts as much as rice.

**Example:** base prices of A, B, C: ₹10, ₹20, ₹40; current prices: ₹12, ₹25, ₹44.
- Aggregative: Σp1 = 81, Σp0 = 70; index = 81/70 × 100 = **115.71**.
- Price relatives: 120, 125, 110; average = 355/3 = **118.33**.

The two methods give different answers — a reminder that the method matters.

**Why units matter in the aggregative method:** suppose B's price is quoted per 10 kg instead of per kg (₹200 → ₹250). Σp1 = 12 + 250 + 44 = 306, Σp0 = 10 + 200 + 40 = 250, index = 122.4 — a different answer from the same price changes, just because of units. The relatives method gives 118.33 either way.

check.q: The price of a good rises from ₹40 to ₹50. Its price relative is:
check.why: Price relative = 50 ÷ 40 × 100 = 125, meaning a 25% rise.

sections.h: Weighted index numbers: Laspeyres and Paasche
sections.md:
A family spends much more on rice than on salt, so a rice price rise hurts more. **Weighted** indices give each item a weight reflecting its importance — usually the **quantity** bought or the **expenditure share**.

**Weighted aggregative method:**

- **Laspeyres' index** uses **base-year quantities** as weights:
 P01 = (Σp1q0 ÷ Σp0q0) × 100
 It answers: how much would the *base-year basket* cost today?

- **Paasche's index** uses **current-year quantities** as weights:
 P01 = (Σp1q1 ÷ Σp0q1) × 100
 It answers: how much more does the *current basket* cost than it would have in the base year?

Laspeyres is easier in practice — base quantities need to be surveyed only once — so most official price indices are Laspeyres-type. It tends to **overstate** price rise slightly, because people shift away from goods that become costly; Paasche tends to understate it. Paasche needs fresh quantity data every period, which is expensive.

**Weighted average of price relatives:**

P01 = Σ(R × W) ÷ ΣW, where R = price relative and W = weight (often expenditure share).

This is the method used for India's CPI and WPI, with weights from household consumption surveys or production values.

sections.md:
Index numbers can measure changes in **quantities**, not just prices. A **quantity index** shows how the physical volume of output or consumption has changed. Here *prices* act as weights, so that a tonne of steel and a tonne of cotton are combined by their values.

**Laspeyres' quantity index:** Q01 = (Σq1p0 ÷ Σq0p0) × 100

**Paasche's quantity index:** Q01 = (Σq1p1 ÷ Σq0p1) × 100

Using the three-good example from the worked problems (A: q0 = 5, q1 = 4; B: 3, 3; C: 2, 2; base prices 10, 20, 40):
Σq1p0 = 40 + 60 + 80 = 180; Σq0p0 = 50 + 60 + 80 = 190. Laspeyres quantity index = 180/190 × 100 ≈ **94.7** — the family is buying about 5% less in volume, mainly because it cut its purchase of A.

The **Index of Industrial Production** is a quantity index: it tracks whether factories, mines and power plants are producing more or less than in the base year.

**Value index:** Σp1q1 ÷ Σp0q0 × 100 compares total spending, mixing price and quantity changes. For our example 211/190 × 100 ≈ 111.1.

check.q: The Index of Industrial Production measures change in:
check.why: IIP is a quantity index tracking the physical volume of production in mining, manufacturing and electricity.

sections.h: Building a price index step by step
sections.md:
Let us build a mini cost-of-living index for a household in Bhopal using the **weighted average of price relatives** — the method behind the CPI.

| Group | Weight (% of spending) | Base price index | Current relative R | R × W |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Food | 50 | 100 | 130 | 6,500 |
| Fuel & light | 10 | 100 | 110 | 1,100 |
| Clothing | 10 | 100 | 120 | 1,200 |
| Rent | 20 | 100 | 150 | 3,000 |
| Miscellaneous | 10 | 100 | 105 | 1,050 |
| Total | 100 | | | 12,850 |

Index = 12,850 ÷ 100 = **128.5**. The family's cost of living has risen 28.5% since the base year.

**Steps in general:**
1. Decide the purpose and the group whose costs you measure.
2. Choose a normal base year.
3. Select representative items and the markets where prices are collected.
4. Collect base and current prices; compute price relatives.
5. Fix weights from a family budget survey.
6. Compute the weighted average.

Notice how rent, with a 20% weight and a 50% rise, contributes far more to the result than fuel.

sections.h: Some important index numbers in India
sections.md:
**Consumer Price Index (CPI)** — measures change in the retail prices of a basket of goods and services bought by households. The NSO publishes **CPI (Rural)**, **CPI (Urban)** and **CPI (Combined)** with base 2012 = 100 (a revision to a newer base year is under way). The Labour Bureau publishes **CPI for Industrial Workers (CPI-IW)** and for agricultural and rural labourers. Food has a large weight (about 46% in CPI-Combined). The **Reserve Bank of India** targets CPI-Combined inflation at 4% (with a band of 2–6%).

**Wholesale Price Index (WPI)** — measures change in prices at the wholesale level: primary articles, fuel and power, manufactured products. Base 2011–12 = 100; published by the Office of the Economic Adviser, Ministry of Commerce and Industry. It excludes services.

**Index of Industrial Production (IIP)** — measures change in the **volume of production** of mining, manufacturing and electricity. Base 2011–12 = 100; published monthly by the NSO.

**Producer Price Index (PPI)** — measures prices received by producers; under development in India to replace or supplement WPI.

**Sensex** — the BSE Sensitive Index of 30 large, actively traded companies on the Bombay Stock Exchange, base 1978–79 = 100. **Nifty 50** is the NSE's index of 50 companies. These track the general mood of the share market.

**Index of Agricultural Production**, and **Human Development Index** (UNDP) are other examples.

sections.md:
Students often mix up the two main price indices. Here is a side-by-side view.

| Basis | CPI | WPI |
|---|---|---|
| Prices used | Retail (what consumers pay) | Wholesale (bulk transactions) |
| Coverage | Goods and services | Goods only |
| Weights from | Household consumption surveys | Value of production/traded output |
| Main use | Cost of living, inflation targeting, DA | Prices at producer/wholesale stage, business contracts |
| Food weight | High (around 46% in CPI-C) | Lower |

Because of these differences, CPI and WPI inflation can move very differently. When global crude oil prices fall, WPI (with a big weight for fuel and manufactured goods) may show low or even negative inflation while CPI stays high because vegetable and service prices keep rising. That is why the RBI moved to targeting CPI inflation: it reflects what households actually feel.

left.title: CPI
points: Used for RBI's inflation target and DA

check.q: Why did the RBI choose CPI rather than WPI for its inflation target?
options: CPI reflects prices households actually pay, including services
check.why: CPI measures the retail cost of goods and services consumers buy, which is what matters for people's purchasing power.

sections.h: Inflation, real wages and other uses
sections.md:
**Inflation rate** = percentage change in a price index:

Inflation = [(Current CPI − Previous CPI) ÷ Previous CPI] × 100.

If CPI rose from 180 to 189 over a year, inflation = 9/180 × 100 = **5%**.

**Real wage (purchasing power).** A worker's money wage rose from ₹20,000 to ₹30,000 while CPI rose from 100 to 150. Real wage = money wage ÷ CPI × 100 = 30,000 ÷ 150 × 100 = **₹20,000** in base-year rupees — no real gain at all! Index numbers thus help settle **dearness allowance (DA)** for government employees, which is linked to CPI-IW.

**Purchasing power of the rupee** = 100 ÷ price index. With CPI 200, ₹1 today buys what 50 paise bought in the base year.

**Deflating national income.** GDP measured at current prices rises both because more is produced and because prices rise. Dividing by a price index (the GDP deflator) gives **real GDP**: if nominal GDP is ₹300 lakh crore and the deflator is 150, real GDP = 300 ÷ 150 × 100 = ₹200 lakh crore at base-year prices.

**Uses of index numbers:**
- Measure inflation and guide RBI's monetary policy.
- Adjust wages, pensions and DA.
- Deflate national income to real terms (GDP at constant prices).
- Help government frame economic policy (taxes, subsidies, minimum support prices).
- Show trends in industrial output and business activity.
- Guide investors via Sensex and Nifty.

sections.h: Issues in constructing an index number
sections.md:
Building a good index needs careful choices:

1. **Purpose** — what exactly do we want to measure? A cost-of-living index for factory workers needs a different basket from a wholesale index.
2. **Choice of base year** — should be a 'normal' year, free of droughts, wars or pandemics, and not too far in the past. That is why base years are revised periodically.
3. **Selection of items** — representative of the group, not too many, of standard quality that can be priced over time.
4. **Selection of prices** — retail or wholesale; from which markets; how often.
5. **Choice of weights** — based on quantity or value; must reflect relative importance.
6. **Choice of average and formula** — Laspeyres, Paasche, weighted relatives.

**Limitations:** indices are approximate; consumption patterns change (smartphones barely existed in old baskets); quality changes are hard to capture; different formulas give different answers; an all-India CPI may not reflect your own family's experience.

**Conclusion.** Index numbers condense the changes in many related variables into a single figure relative to a base of 100. Simple methods are easy but crude; weighted methods (Laspeyres, Paasche, weighted relatives) reflect importance. India's CPI, WPI, IIP and Sensex are index numbers that shape policy, wages and investment. Building them requires careful choices of purpose, base, items, prices, weights and formula — and reading them requires knowing what they do and do not measure.

> Did you know? When new products become important — like mobile phone charges — statisticians must revise the basket, which is one reason India updates base years every decade or so.

parts.md: While cleaning the loft in their Kanpur home, Aryan found his grandmother's old diary from the year he was born. Every month she had noted the price of rice, dal, cooking oil, milk and the electricity bill. 'Look, Dadi — milk was so cheap!' he said. She smiled: 'And my pension was smaller too. Is today really costlier?'

Aryan made a table: base prices from the diary, current prices from the grocery app, and the quantities Dadi used to buy each month as weights. He computed price relatives — milk 180, rice 160, oil 150, dal 170, electricity 140 — and a Laspeyres index of about 162. Her pension, meanwhile, had gone up from ₹12,000 to ₹21,000 — a rise to 175 on the same base.

'So your real pension rose a little, Dadi,' Aryan concluded: 21,000 ÷ 162 × 100 ≈ ₹12,963 in old rupees, compared with ₹12,000 then. Dadi laughed, 'So the government's DA did its job.' Aryan realised that the CPI he read about in newspapers was simply a giant, carefully built version of Dadi's diary.

sections.h: A question on a train window
sections.md:
Imagine the Rajdhani pulling out of New Delhi at dusk and rolling east towards Howrah. Through the window the land changes slowly: wheat and mustard fields of western Uttar Pradesh, the brick kilns near Kanpur, the wide sandy bed of the Ganga at Prayagraj, the paddy fields and ponds of Bihar, and finally the crowded, humid, river-cut plain of Bengal. Nothing about that journey is random. Why is rice grown more as you go east? Why are the villages bigger and closer together? Why do houses in Bengal have sloping roofs while those near Delhi have flat ones?

Every one of those questions is a **geographical question**. Geography asks *what* is found *where*, *why* it is found there, and *how* places are connected to each other. The word itself comes from Greek: *geo* (earth) and *graphein* (to describe or write). The Greek scholar **Eratosthenes** (3rd century BCE) is usually credited with first using the word. But geography today is far more than describing the Earth. It is about explaining it.

This chapter is the doorway to the whole Class 11 course. It answers big questions:

1. What exactly is geography, and what makes it different from other subjects?
2. How is it linked to the natural and social sciences?
3. How have geographers studied the Earth — what approaches have they used?
4. What are the branches of geography, and how does physical geography fit in and why does it matter?

> Did you know? The surface of the Earth is never the same in two places. Even two neighbouring villages differ in soil, water table and slope. Geography is the science of that variation.

sections.h: Geography is about variation, and it is dynamic
sections.md:
Look around your own town. The houses near the river are built on stilts or raised plinths; those on the hill are not. The market sits where two roads meet. Rich farmland lies on one side of the canal and dry scrub on the other. The Earth's surface is **not uniform** — it varies in physical features (relief, soil, climate, water, vegetation) and in cultural features (houses, roads, crops, languages, dress). Geography studies these variations and tries to explain them.

The NCERT chapter stresses three kinds of questions geographers ask:

- **What?** — identifying the features found on the Earth's surface (natural and cultural).
- **Where?** — locating them and describing their distribution.
- **Why?** — explaining the causes behind those distributions and the links between features.

The 'why' question makes geography a **scientific** discipline rather than a list of place-names. When a geographer notes that rice is grown more as rainfall rises eastward across the Ganga plain, she is not stopping at description; she is identifying a **cause-and-effect** relationship.

Geography is also **dynamic**. The relationship between people and nature changes over time, mainly through **technology**. Long ago, communities in a hill forest lived by gathering and shifting cultivation, fearing floods and wild animals. Today the same valley may have a dam, a highway, terraced orchards and mobile towers. Nature has been 'humanised' — but nature still sets limits, as landslides on cut slopes remind us. Because both the physical environment and human society keep changing, the geography of any place is always being rewritten.

check.q: Which question makes geography an explanatory, scientific discipline?
check.why: Asking why features are distributed as they are leads to cause-and-effect explanation, which is the scientific core of geography.

sections.md:
Most school subjects slice the world by *type of thing*. Botany studies plants, economics studies production and exchange, sociology studies society. Geography slices the world differently — by **space**. It studies how all those things come together in a particular place and how they vary from place to place.

Think of your own district. Its rainfall (climatology), its soils (pedology), its crops (agriculture), its roads and markets (economics), its castes, languages and festivals (sociology) and its history of settlement (history) all sit on the same patch of ground and influence each other. A geographer looks at how they are **interrelated** in that space. That is why geography is called an **integrating discipline** — a synthesis of many fields.

There are three ways of looking at reality:

- **Time** — studied by history. History asks *when* and *in what order*.
- **Space** — studied by geography. Geography asks *where* and *how distributed*.
- **Category of things** — studied by systematic sciences like botany, geology, economics.

History and geography are therefore twins. Every event happens somewhere; every place has a past. Changes in a place over time — a forest becoming farmland, a village becoming a suburb — need both lenses.

**Spatial distribution and association.** Two key ideas make geography scientific. First, *distribution*: where is something found and how does its density change? Second, *association*: what other things vary along with it? For example, the map of high population density in India closely matches the map of fertile alluvial plains and assured water. Finding such associations — and then explaining them through **cause-and-effect** — is the heart of geographical work.

**Maps** are the geographer's special tool. A map lets you see distributions and associations at a glance — overlay a rainfall map on a crop map and the link jumps out. That is why it is said that geography cannot be done without maps.

check.why: Geography studies how phenomena are distributed and interrelated across space, just as history studies them across time.

sections.h: Physical geography and the natural sciences; human geography and the social sciences
sections.md:
Geography stands with one foot in the natural sciences and one in the social sciences. The textbook spells out these links.

**Physical geography and natural sciences.** All branches of physical geography have close ties with natural sciences:
- **Geomorphology** draws on **geology** — rocks, structure and earth processes.
- **Climatology** draws on **meteorology** and atmospheric **physics** — heat, pressure, winds.
- **Hydrology** and **oceanography** draw on physics and chemistry of water.
- **Soil geography** draws on **pedology** and chemistry.
- **Biogeography** draws on **botany**, **zoology** and **ecology**.
- **Mathematics** is needed for map projections, surveying and statistical techniques; **astronomy** helps explain latitude, longitude, time zones and seasons.

**Human geography and social sciences.** Every social science has a matching branch of geography:

| Social science | Branch of geography |
|---|---|
| History | Historical geography |
| Sociology | Social geography |
| Political science | Political geography |
| Economics | Economic geography |
| Demography | Population geography |

The difference is in the lens. An economist studies *how* markets work; an economic geographer studies *where* industries are located and why — why textile mills clustered around Mumbai and Ahmedabad, or IT firms around Bengaluru. A political scientist studies the working of a state; a political geographer studies its boundaries, constituencies and the influence of location on power.

This double link is what lets geography explain a place completely: the physical setting *and* the human use of it, studied together.

check.q: Economic geography differs from economics mainly because it focuses on:
options: The location and spatial pattern of economic activities
check.why: Economic geography asks where economic activities happen and why, adding the spatial lens to economic study.

sections.h: Nature and humans: the great debate
sections.md:
How much does nature shape human life, and how much do humans shape nature? Geographers have argued about this for over a century. Three positions are useful to know.

**1. Environmental determinism.** In early stages of technology, people depended heavily on their surroundings. Nature seemed all-powerful: it decided what people ate, wore and built. Determinists argued that climate and terrain *determine* human behaviour and even culture. The German geographer **Friedrich Ratzel** and the American **Ellen Churchill Semple** are associated with this view. The problem: it explains too little. Two places with the same climate can have very different societies.

**2. Possibilism.** As technology grew, humans began to choose among the possibilities that nature offers. The French school led by **Paul Vidal de la Blache** emphasised this: nature offers opportunities, and humans pick. Terraced fields on Himalayan slopes, canals in the Thar, cities built on reclaimed sea in Mumbai — all show human choice. Possibilists see a *humanised* nature with the imprint of human effort everywhere.

**3. Neo-determinism (stop-and-go determinism).** The geographer **Griffith Taylor** proposed a middle path. Humans can modify nature, but only within limits. Like a driver at a traffic signal, we can go fast when the light is green, but if we ignore red lights — by over-pumping groundwater, cutting forests on steep slopes, building on floodplains — nature punishes us. Neither total freedom nor total slavery: we must read the signals.

Today's ideas of **sustainable development** are close to neo-determinism. Floods in a city built over its own drains, or a groundwater crisis in Punjab after decades of paddy, are reminders that the light turned red.

check.q: The idea that humans can modify nature but must respect its limits, like obeying traffic lights, is called:
check.why: Griffith Taylor's neo-determinism, or stop-and-go determinism, accepts human choice within limits set by nature.

sections.h: How geography grew: from description to science
sections.md:
Geography's methods have changed many times. It helps to see the broad sequence as a timeline.

- **Early colonial period:** explorers and travellers described new lands for empires — routes, resources, peoples. Geography was mainly *exploration and description*.
- **Later colonial period:** **regional analysis** became important. The idea was that understanding each region in detail, then adding the regions up, explains the whole.
- **Inter-war period (1918–1939):** **areal differentiation** — identifying how and why one region differs from another.
- **1950s–1960s:** **spatial organisation** and the **quantitative revolution**. Geographers used statistics, mathematical models and maps to find laws. This is also called the positivist approach.
- **1970s:** reaction against pure numbers — **humanistic**, **radical** (Marxian) and **behavioural** schools. They asked about human feelings, inequality and decision-making.
- **1990s onwards:** **post-modernism** questioned grand theories and stressed local context.

India has its own long geographical tradition. Ancient texts describe *dvipas* (continents), rivers and mountains; Puranic geography describes Jambudvipa; travellers such as Al-Biruni recorded Indian geography; Aryabhata and Varahamihira wrote on astronomy linked to the Earth. Mapping of India by the **Survey of India** (founded 1767) and the **Great Trigonometrical Survey** that measured the height of Mount Everest in the 19th century were landmarks in scientific geography.

fig.caption: Broad phases in the development of geographical thought.

check.q: The quantitative revolution in geography is associated mainly with:
check.why: In the 1950s–60s geographers adopted statistics and models to seek general spatial laws, which is called the quantitative revolution.

sections.md:
**The systematic approach** was introduced by the German geographer **Alexander von Humboldt** (1769–1859). Here you take one phenomenon — say, climate — and study it across the whole world: how it varies, what causes the patterns, and then you classify it into types (tropical wet, desert, Mediterranean…). Then you move to the next phenomenon. It is *topic-first*.

**The regional approach** was developed by **Karl Ritter** (1779–1859), a contemporary of Humboldt. Here you divide the world into regions at different levels — continent, country, state, district — and study *all* the phenomena of one region together: its landforms, climate, vegetation, economy and culture, and how they combine to give that region its personality. It is *place-first*.

| Question | Systematic | Regional |
|---|---|---|
| Starting point | One theme (e.g., soils) | One region (e.g., Kerala) |
| Method | Compare that theme across the world | Combine all themes within the region |
| Output | Types and laws | Regional personality |

Both need each other. A regional study of Kerala needs systematic knowledge of monsoon climatology; a systematic study of rice farming needs examples from regions like Kerala, Punjab and the Mekong delta. The textbook stresses that the two are **complementary**, not opposed — the dichotomy (split) between them is more apparent than real.

> Did you know? Humboldt and Ritter were both German and died in the same year, 1859 — the year Darwin published *On the Origin of Species*.
keyTerms: Systematic geography — theme-wise study across the globe
Regional geography — region-wise study of all phenomena together

check.q: Who is associated with the regional approach to geography?
check.why: Karl Ritter developed the regional approach, while Alexander von Humboldt introduced the systematic approach.

sections.md:
**Based on the systematic approach**, geography divides into four main parts:

**1. Physical geography**
- *Geomorphology* — landforms, their evolution and processes.
- *Climatology* — structure of the atmosphere and elements of weather and climate.
- *Hydrology* — water on the Earth: oceans, lakes, rivers, and its effects on life.
- *Soil geography* — soil formation, types, fertility and distribution.

**2. Human geography**
- *Social/cultural geography* — society, its dynamics and culture.
- *Population and settlement geography* — population growth, distribution, density, migration; rural and urban settlements.
- *Economic geography* — economic activities: agriculture, industry, tourism, trade, transport and infrastructure.
- *Historical geography* — how areas were organised and developed through history.
- *Political geography* — boundaries, electoral constituencies, geopolitics.

**3. Biogeography** (the interface of physical and human geography)
- *Plant geography* and *zoogeography* — distribution of plants and animals.
- *Ecology/ecosystem* — scientific study of habitats and interactions.
- *Environmental geography* — environmental problems such as land degradation and pollution, and conservation.

**4. Geographical methods and techniques**
- *Cartography* (map making), *quantitative techniques* (statistics), *field survey*, and *geo-informatics* — **remote sensing, GIS and GPS**.

**Based on the regional approach**, the branches are: **regional studies/area studies** (macro, meso, micro), **regional planning** (country/rural/town planning), **regional development**, and **regional analysis**.

Finally, two aspects are common to every discipline: **philosophy** — **geographical thought** and **human–environment interaction / human ecology** — and **methods and techniques**.

Geo-informatics has transformed the field. A satellite image from ISRO's Resourcesat can show crop health across a state; GIS overlays it with rainfall and roads; a GPS-enabled phone helps a field worker verify on the ground. Disaster managers used these tools during cyclones like Fani (2019) to evacuate people in time.

sections.h: Physical geography and why it matters
sections.md:
This whole textbook is about physical geography, so the chapter ends by explaining its importance.

Physical geography studies the four great realms of the Earth:

- **Lithosphere** — landforms, drainage, relief and the rocks beneath.
- **Atmosphere** — composition, structure, weather and climate, winds and pressure.
- **Hydrosphere** — oceans, seas, lakes and all the water on Earth.
- **Biosphere** — life forms including humans, and the processes that sustain them (food chains, ecological balance).

Why should a student of humanities care? Because every human activity rests on these realms.

- **Landforms** provide the base for farms, roads, railways and cities. Plains favour agriculture; slopes favour plantations or forests; mountains create barriers but also tourism and hydropower.
- **Climate** decides our houses, clothes and food. A Rajasthani turban and a Kashmiri pheran are both climatic adaptations.
- **Soils** are renewable only very slowly; their loss through erosion is a loss for generations.
- **Oceans** supply fish, salt, minerals and trade routes; they moderate climate.
- **The biosphere** is the web of life on which our food, medicine and air depend.

Physical geography is thus the stage on which the human drama is performed. Understanding it helps us manage resources sustainably and plan for hazards. Over-use of groundwater, encroachment on floodplains or deforestation on hill slopes all ignore physical geography and bring disaster.

> Did you know? Soils take hundreds of years to form a few centimetres, but heavy monsoon rain on a bare slope can wash that away in one season.

sections.h: Doing geography: a field study of your own locality
sections.md:
The best way to understand geography as a discipline is to *do* it. Here is a simple project that uses every idea in this chapter.

1. **Choose a small area** — your ward, village or the 2 km around your school (regional approach, micro level).
2. **Observe physical features** — slope, soil colour, drains, trees, water bodies (physical geography).
3. **Observe cultural features** — houses, roads, shops, farms, places of worship, bus stops (human geography).
4. **Map them** — draw a sketch map with a north arrow and a rough scale, or use a free online map and GPS on a phone (methods and techniques).
5. **Look for associations** — Are shops clustered at road crossings? Are newer houses on higher ground? Is waterlogging found in low-lying lanes?
6. **Ask why** — Talk to elders about how the area has changed in 30 years (historical geography, the dynamic nature of geography).
7. **Think neo-deterministically** — Where have people ignored nature's 'red lights' — filled ponds, blocked drains, cut slopes? What happened?

You will find that you have used systematic ideas (drainage, soils, land use) inside a regional study — exactly the complementarity the chapter describes.

**Conclusion of the chapter.** Geography studies the Earth as the home of humans: what is found where and why, and how places interact. It integrates natural and social sciences through the lens of space, uses maps and techniques to study distributions and associations, and is organised by systematic and regional approaches. Physical geography — the study of land, air, water and life — is the foundation on which human geography is built, and its understanding is essential for sustainable living.

parts.md: Anu, a Class 11 student in Guwahati, had two maps for her project: one showing where floods struck Assam in the last monsoon, the other showing population density. She noticed something strange — the most crowded districts were the ones that flooded most. Why would people live where the river attacks every year?

Her geography teacher suggested a third map — soil fertility. The same belt along the Brahmaputra had the richest alluvial soil, renewed each year by flood silt. Paddy, jute and fish ponds thrived there. 'Here is spatial association,' he said. 'Floods, fertile soil and dense population are found together. The river gives and the river takes.'

Anu wrote in her conclusion that people had chosen to live with the river (possibilism), but embankments built carelessly and wetlands filled for housing had made floods worse (ignoring the red light of neo-determinism). She proposed raised plinths, early-warning by satellite, and protecting wetlands. Without knowing it, she had used every idea in Chapter 1.

summary: Geography comes from Greek geo (earth) + graphein (describe); Eratosthenes is credited with the term.
Geography studies variation of the Earth's surface and asks what, where and why.
Geography is dynamic — the people–environment relationship changes with technology.
Geography studies phenomena across space; history across time; systematic sciences by category.
Geography is an integrating discipline bridging natural and social sciences; maps are its key tool.
Each branch of physical geography links with a natural science; each social science has a matching branch of human geography.
Spatial distribution, spatial association and cause-and-effect explanation are central.
Environmental determinism (Ratzel, Semple), possibilism (Vidal de la Blache) and neo-determinism (Griffith Taylor) describe the human–nature relationship.
Approaches evolved from exploration to regional analysis, areal differentiation, quantitative revolution, humanistic/radical/behavioural and post-modern schools.
Systematic approach (Humboldt) is theme-first; regional approach (Ritter) is place-first; they are complementary.
Main systematic branches: physical, human, biogeography, and methods and techniques; regional branches: regional studies, planning, development, analysis.
Geo-informatics: remote sensing, GIS, GPS.
Physical geography studies lithosphere, atmosphere, hydrosphere and biosphere and underpins all human activity.

rd-school-c11-geography.ch2-origin-evolu.title: The Origin and Evolution of the Earth
rd-school-c11-geography.ch2-origin-evolu.subtitle: From a spinning cloud of dust to a blue planet with oceans, air and life

sections.h: Where did the ground beneath your feet come from?
sections.md:
Pick up a pebble from the bed of the Narmada. The atoms in it — silicon, oxygen, iron, calcium — were not made on Earth. They were forged inside stars that lived and died before our Sun was born. The pebble is, quite literally, recycled stardust. How did that dust become a planet with mountains, oceans, an atmosphere and living beings who ask questions about it?

This chapter tells that story in three acts:

1. **The origin of the universe** — early theories and the Big Bang.
2. **The formation of stars and planets**, including our solar system and the Moon.
3. **The evolution of the Earth** — layering of its interior, the making of the atmosphere and oceans, and the origin of life.

Along the way you will meet early hypotheses that scientists later rejected. That is not a weakness of science; it is how science works. Each idea is tested against evidence and replaced if a better one explains more.

> Did you know? The universe is about 13.7–13.8 billion years old, the Earth about 4.6 billion years old. If the whole history of the universe were squeezed into one year, the Earth would form around the end of August or early September and humans would appear in the last few minutes of 31 December.

sections.h: Early theories of the Earth's origin
sections.md:
For centuries, people explained the origin of the Earth through religious and mythological stories. Scientific hypotheses began in the 18th century.

**Nebular hypothesis.** The German philosopher **Immanuel Kant** proposed that the planets formed from a cloud of material. In **1796** the French mathematician **Pierre-Simon Laplace** revised it: a slowly rotating, hot cloud of gas (a *nebula*) associated with a youthful Sun cooled and contracted; as it spun faster, rings of material were thrown off, and these condensed into planets.

**Gaseous tidal / binary star hypotheses.** Later, in **1900, Chamberlin and Moulton** suggested that a wandering star approached the Sun and pulled out a cigar-shaped filament of material by tidal force. As the star moved away, this material kept revolving around the Sun and condensed into planets. **Sir James Jeans** and later **Sir Harold Jeffrey** supported versions of this idea. Some versions also involved a companion star to the Sun — the *binary theory*.

**Revised nebular hypothesis.** In **1950, Otto Schmidt** (Russia) and **Carl Weizascar** (Germany) revised the nebular idea. They proposed that the Sun was surrounded by a **solar nebula** made mostly of hydrogen and helium along with dust. Friction and collisions of particles formed a disc-shaped cloud, and the planets formed by **accretion** — particles sticking together.

The modern view keeps the core of the nebular idea, because it explains why all planets orbit the Sun in nearly the same plane and the same direction.

> Note: The textbook spells the German scientist's name as 'Carl Weizascar'; in physics books you will see Carl Friedrich von Weizsäcker.

items.what: Kant's idea of planets from a cloud
Chamberlin and Moulton: wandering star pulls out material
Hubble: galaxies moving apart — expanding universe
Otto Schmidt and Weizsäcker: revised nebular hypothesis

fig.caption: Milestones in ideas about the origin of the Earth and universe.

check.q: Who revised the nebular hypothesis in 1796?
check.why: Laplace in 1796 revised Kant's idea into the nebular hypothesis of a rotating, cooling gas cloud.

sections.md:
Modern scientists no longer think about the Earth alone; they ask where the whole universe came from. The most widely accepted explanation is the **Big Bang Theory**, also called the **expanding universe hypothesis**.

In **1920, Edwin Hubble** provided evidence that the universe is expanding: galaxies are moving away from each other, and the farther they are, the faster they recede. The balloon analogy helps — draw dots on a balloon and blow it up; every dot moves away from every other dot. Note the subtlety: the dots (galaxies) do not themselves grow; the space between them does.

The Big Bang Theory describes the following stages:

1. In the beginning, all matter forming the universe existed in **one place as a tiny ball** (a singular atom) with unimaginably small volume, infinite temperature and infinite density.
2. At the Big Bang, this tiny ball exploded violently, leading to a huge expansion. This expansion continues today. Scientists believe it happened **about 13.7 billion years ago**. As the universe grew, some energy was converted into matter. Expansion was extremely rapid within fractions of a second after the bang and slowed thereafter.
3. Within the first **three minutes** after the Big Bang, the first atoms began to form.
4. Within **300,000 years**, temperature dropped to about **4,500 K** and atomic matter formed. The universe became transparent.

The expansion of the universe means an increase in space between galaxies. An alternative, the **steady state concept** of **Hoyle**, held that the universe was roughly the same at any point of time. But growing evidence favours the Big Bang.

sections.h: How do scientists know? The evidence
sections.md:
No one was present at the Big Bang or at the birth of the Earth. So how can scientists speak of dates in billions of years? Several independent lines of evidence point to the same story.

- **Redshift of galaxies.** Light from distant galaxies is stretched towards the red end of the spectrum, just as the sound of a train horn drops in pitch as it moves away. Hubble used this to show that galaxies are receding — the universe is expanding. Run the expansion backwards and everything converges to one point.
- **Cosmic microwave background (CMB).** In 1965 two radio engineers detected a faint microwave 'hiss' coming from every direction in the sky. It is the cooled afterglow of the hot early universe, released when atoms formed — exactly what the Big Bang predicts and what the steady state idea cannot explain well.
- **Abundance of light elements.** The universe is about three-quarters hydrogen and one-quarter helium by mass — the proportions predicted for the first minutes after the Big Bang.
- **Radiometric dating.** Radioactive elements such as uranium decay into lead at a fixed, known rate. Measuring how much has decayed in a rock gives its age, like a natural clock. The oldest meteorites — leftovers from the solar nebula — date to about 4.56 billion years, giving the age of the solar system and Earth.
- **Moon rocks and Earth's oldest minerals.** Tiny zircon crystals from Western Australia are about 4.4 billion years old, showing that a solid crust existed early.

When many different methods give the same answer, scientists gain confidence. That is why the Big Bang and the nebular origin of the solar system are accepted today, while older ideas have been set aside.

sections.h: The star formation and the planets
sections.md:
Matter and energy were not spread perfectly evenly in the early universe. These tiny differences in density created **gravitational pull** that drew matter together. These clumps became the seeds of **galaxies**. A galaxy contains a huge number of stars; distances are so vast that they are measured in **light years** — the distance light travels in one year, about **9.461 × 10¹² km**. A single galaxy may be 80,000 to 150,000 light years across.

A galaxy begins as a huge cloud of hydrogen gas called a **nebula**. Within it, localised clumps of gas grow denser, and these become **stars**. Star formation is believed to have taken place some **5–6 billion years ago**.

**Formation of planets** happens in stages:

1. Stars are localised lumps of gas within a nebula. Gravity inside the lumps leads to formation of a core, surrounded by a rotating disc of gas and dust.
2. The gas cloud condenses, and matter around the core forms small rounded objects. Through cohesion, these become **planetesimals**. Larger bodies start forming by collision and gravitational attraction.
3. Many small planetesimals **accrete** to form a few large bodies — the **planets**.

**Our solar system** has eight planets. The nebula from which it formed began collapsing and forming a core around 5–5.6 billion years ago, and the planets formed about **4.6 billion years ago**. The solar system includes the Sun, eight planets, about 63 moons (the textbook's figure; many more are now known), millions of smaller bodies like asteroids and comets, and huge quantities of dust and gas.

The planets fall into two groups:

| Feature | Inner (terrestrial) | Outer (Jovian / gas giants) |
|---|---|---|
| Planets | Mercury, Venus, Earth, Mars | Jupiter, Saturn, Uranus, Neptune |
| Composition | Rock and metal; high density | Mostly gases (H, He); low density |
| Size | Small | Huge |
| Atmosphere | Thin, much lost | Thick, retained |

Why the difference? (a) Terrestrial planets formed close to the parent star, where it was too warm for gases to condense. (b) The solar wind near the Sun blew away much gas and dust from the inner region. (c) Being small, terrestrial planets had weaker gravity and could not hold escaping gases.

*Terrestrial* means Earth-like (from Latin *terra*, earth); *Jovian* means Jupiter-like (from Jove, another name for Jupiter).

sections.md:
The Moon is Earth's only natural satellite. Early ideas included one by **Sir George Darwin** (1838) — that Earth and Moon were once a single rapidly rotating body that split into a dumb-bell shape and broke apart; it was even suggested that the Pacific Ocean was the hollow left behind. This is no longer accepted.

The present view is the **giant impact** or *big splat* hypothesis. Shortly after the Earth formed, a body about **one to three times the size of Mars** collided with it. The impact blasted a large part of Earth's outer material into space. This material went into orbit and gathered together to form the Moon, about **4.44 billion years ago**.

Evidence supporting it: Moon rocks brought back by Apollo missions are chemically similar to Earth's mantle; the Moon has a small iron core (the impactor's iron largely merged into Earth); and computer models reproduce the Earth–Moon system well.

India's **Chandrayaan-1** (2008) helped detect water molecules on the lunar surface, and **Chandrayaan-3** (2023) landed near the lunar south pole, studying its soil and temperature — modern chapters in the same story.

> Did you know? The Moon is slowly moving away from the Earth by about 3.8 cm every year, measured by bouncing lasers off reflectors left by astronauts.

sections.h: Evolution of the Earth: layers, air and oceans
sections.md:
The early Earth was barren, rocky and hot, with a thin atmosphere of hydrogen and helium. It took hundreds of millions of years to become the planet we know.

**Development of lithosphere.** The Earth was mostly in a volatile state at first. Gradual increase in density raised the temperature inside. Material began to separate by density: **heavier materials like iron sank towards the centre**, lighter ones moved towards the surface. With time it cooled further, solidified and condensed. This process of separation is called **differentiation**. It formed layers: **crust, mantle, outer core and inner core**, density increasing from crust to core. Later, after the Moon-forming impact, the Earth heated up again and a second round of differentiation occurred.

**Evolution of atmosphere and hydrosphere.** The present atmosphere is composed chiefly of nitrogen and oxygen. Three stages are recognised:

1. **Loss of the primordial atmosphere** — the early hydrogen and helium were stripped away by the **solar winds**. This happened to all terrestrial planets.
2. **Contribution of the hot interior** — as Earth cooled, gases and water vapour escaped from the interior through volcanoes. This **degassing** produced an atmosphere rich in water vapour, nitrogen, carbon dioxide, methane and ammonia, with very little free oxygen.
3. **Modification by living organisms** — through **photosynthesis**.

Continuous volcanic eruptions added water vapour. As Earth cooled, the vapour condensed; carbon dioxide dissolved in rainwater, lowering temperature and causing more condensation and more rain. Rainwater collected in depressions to form **oceans**. The oceans formed **within 500 million years** of Earth's formation — so they are as old as about **4,000 million years**.

Around **3,800 million years ago** life began to evolve. Around **2,500–3,000 million years ago** photosynthesis evolved. Life was confined to oceans for a long time. Oceans began to fill with oxygen released by photosynthesis, and eventually oceans were saturated; around **2,000 million years ago** oxygen began flooding the atmosphere.

check.why: Differentiation is the sinking of heavier materials toward the centre and rising of lighter ones, creating Earth's layers.

sections.md:
The last stage of the Earth's evolution is the origin and evolution of life. The early atmosphere was not conducive to life as we know it. Modern scientists consider the origin of life a kind of **chemical reaction**: first, complex organic molecules formed from simpler ones, then they assembled into self-copying structures — converting inanimate matter into living substance.

The record of life is found in rocks as **fossils**. Microscopic structures closely related to present-day **blue-green algae** have been found in geological formations **much older than 3,000 million years**. It can be assumed that life began to evolve sometime **3,800 million years ago**.

The geological time scale divides Earth's history into **eons, eras, periods and epochs**:

| Eon | Era | Notable life |
|---|---|---|
| Precambrian (Hadean, Archean, Proterozoic) | — | 4,600–570 mya: soft-bodied life, blue-green algae, first single cells |
| Phanerozoic | Palaeozoic (570–245 mya) | Fish, first land plants, amphibians, reptiles |
| Phanerozoic | Mesozoic (245–65 mya) | Dinosaurs, first birds and mammals |
| Phanerozoic | Cainozoic (65 mya–present) | Mammals, primates, humans (Holocene: modern humans) |

(mya = million years ago; figures follow the NCERT table.)

A powerful way to feel this scale: if Earth's 4.6 billion years were a 24-hour day starting at midnight, the oceans appear around 3 am, photosynthesis between about 8 and 11 am, the dinosaurs arrive near 10:45 pm and vanish by about 11:40 pm, and the whole of human history fits into the last few seconds.

> Did you know? Stromatolites — layered rocks built by ancient microbes — are still forming today in Shark Bay, Australia, and fossil stromatolites are found in India's Aravalli and Vindhyan rocks.

sections.h: Why the Earth became a living planet
sections.md:
Our solar system has three rocky neighbours — Venus, Earth and Mars — that began from similar material. Why did only Earth become a world of forests, oceans and people? Putting this chapter's ideas together gives an answer.

- **Right distance from the Sun.** Earth lies in a zone where water can stay **liquid** on the surface. Venus, closer in, became a runaway greenhouse with surface temperatures over 450 °C; Mars, farther out and small, lost most of its air and its water froze or escaped.
- **Right size.** Earth's gravity is strong enough to hold an atmosphere of nitrogen and oxygen (recall why small inner planets lost gases).
- **A hot, layered interior.** Differentiation gave Earth an iron core whose motion creates a **magnetic field**. This shield deflects the solar wind that stripped away the primordial atmosphere — protecting the second atmosphere made by degassing.
- **Oceans as a cradle.** Oceans formed early, absorbed carbon dioxide and gave life a protected home for over two billion years.
- **Life changed the air.** Photosynthesis released oxygen, which later formed the **ozone layer** that shields land life from ultraviolet rays. Only then could plants and animals move onto land.
- **A large Moon.** The Moon steadies the tilt of Earth's axis, keeping seasons fairly stable over long periods, and raises tides.

**Conclusion of the chapter.** The story runs from a singular point exploding about 13.7 billion years ago, to galaxies and stars forming from nebulae, to planets accreting from planetesimals 4.6 billion years ago, to a giant impact making the Moon. On Earth, differentiation built the layers, degassing and rain built the atmosphere and oceans, and life, through photosynthesis, transformed the air. The next chapter goes inside the Earth to see how we know what those layers are like.

check.q: Which feature of Earth, produced by its iron core, protects its atmosphere from the solar wind?
check.why: Movement in Earth's iron core generates a magnetic field that deflects charged particles of the solar wind.

story.title: The cosmic calendar on the classroom wall

parts.md: Ms. Iyer in Chennai pinned twelve chart papers along the classroom wall — January to December — and told Class 11: 'This wall is the whole history of the universe, 13.8 billion years. Each day is about 38 million years. Let us place our events.' Kavya stuck a gold star on 1 January, just after midnight: the Big Bang.

Galaxies took their places in the early months. Then the class waited… and waited. Only around 31 August did Arjun pin up a small blue Earth, and a grey Moon a few days later. Oceans arrived in mid-September and the first microbes in late September. The students were stunned at how much of the wall was empty of life.

Dinosaurs appeared on Christmas Day and vanished on 30 December. On 31 December, at about 11:52 pm, the first modern humans appeared. 'All of recorded history — the Harappans, the Mauryas, the freedom struggle, your phones — fits in the last 15 seconds,' Ms. Iyer said. The class was silent. 'And we are the only ones on this wall who can read it.'

rd-school-c11-geography.ch3-interior-ear.title: Interior of the Earth
rd-school-c11-geography.ch3-interior-ear.subtitle: No one has dug deeper than 12 km — so how do we know what lies 6,370 km below?

sections.h: The deepest hole and the biggest mystery
sections.md:
The deepest hole humans have ever drilled is the Kola Superdeep Borehole in Russia — about **12.2 km**. The Earth's radius is about **6,370 km**. That means our deepest drill has scratched less than 0.2 per cent of the way to the centre, like a mosquito bite on an apple. Deep mines, like the gold mines of South Africa or the old Kolar Gold Fields in Karnataka, go only 3–4 km down.

Yet geography textbooks confidently describe a crust, a mantle and a core, give their thicknesses and even say the inner core is solid. How do we know? The answer is a wonderful piece of scientific detective work using **indirect evidence** — especially earthquake waves that travel through the planet like X-rays through a body.

Why should a humanities student care? Because the interior drives everything at the surface: earthquakes that shake Delhi and Gujarat, volcanoes in the Andaman islands (Barren Island is India's only active volcano), the rise of the Himalaya, and the shape of continents. Landforms are the result of two sets of processes — **endogenic** (from inside the Earth) and **exogenic** (from outside, like rivers and wind). This chapter is about understanding the inside. It covers:

1. Sources of information about the interior.
2. Earthquakes — waves, their propagation, shadow zones, types, measurement and effects.
3. The structure of the Earth — crust, mantle, core.
4. Volcanoes and volcanic landforms.

sections.h: Sources of information: direct and indirect
sections.md:
**Direct sources**
- **Surface rock and mining.** Rocks exposed at the surface and material from mines tell us about the upper crust. Mining and drilling projects such as the **Deep Ocean Drilling Project** and the **Integrated Ocean Drilling Project** reached a few kilometres.
- **Volcanic eruptions.** Magma that erupts brings material from deeper levels. But we cannot be sure exactly how deep it came from.

**Indirect sources**
- **Temperature, pressure and density.** In mines, temperature and pressure increase with depth — near the surface, temperature typically rises by roughly 25–30 °C per km. Using such rates, scientists estimate values at greater depths. We also know the total thickness of the Earth and its average density, so density must increase sharply inside — surface rocks are about 2.7–3 g/cm³ while the Earth's average is about 5.5 g/cm³.
- **Meteors.** Meteorites that reach the Earth are made of similar material to the Earth's interior, because they formed from the same nebula. Iron-nickel meteorites suggest what the core might be made of.
- **Gravitation.** The pull of gravity (g) is greater near the poles and less at the equator, because of distance from the centre. It also varies with the mass of material below. These differences are called **gravity anomalies**, and they reveal how mass is distributed in the crust.
- **Magnetic surveys** give information about the distribution of magnetic material in the crust.
- **Seismic activity** — by far the most important source. Study of earthquake waves (seismology) gives a complete picture of the layered interior.

> Did you know? Gravity measurements by satellites now track even the shrinking of groundwater under north India, because the loss of water reduces local mass slightly.
keyTerms: Gravity anomaly — difference between expected and observed gravity, showing mass distribution
Seismology — scientific study of earthquake waves

check.q: Which is the most important indirect source of information about the Earth's interior?
check.why: Earthquake waves pass through the whole Earth, and their behaviour reveals the layers they travel through.

sections.md:
An **earthquake** is simply shaking of the Earth. It is caused by release of energy, which generates waves that travel in all directions. Rocks along a **fault** (a fracture in the crust) are locked by friction; stress builds up until they slip suddenly, releasing energy.

The point where energy is released is the **focus** or **hypocentre**. The point on the surface directly above it is the **epicentre** — the first place to experience the waves. All natural earthquakes take place in the lithosphere (up to about 200 km depth).

**Earthquake waves** are of two types:

**Body waves** are generated by the release of energy at the focus and move in all directions through the body of the Earth.
- **P-waves (primary)** move fastest and arrive first. They are like sound waves — they cause the material to compress and expand in the direction of travel (*longitudinal*). They can travel through **solid, liquid and gas**.
- **S-waves (secondary)** arrive later. They make the material vibrate at right angles to the direction of travel (*transverse*), like a shaken rope. They can travel **only through solids**.

**Surface waves** are produced when body waves interact with surface rocks. They move along the surface, arrive last at the seismograph and are the **most destructive**, causing rocks to displace and buildings to collapse.

Waves change speed as they pass through materials of different density; they **reflect** (bounce back) and **refract** (bend) at boundaries. That is how layers were detected. Instruments called **seismographs** record waves arriving at a station.

sections.h: Propagation of earthquake waves and the seismograph
sections.md:
Different waves move the ground in different ways, and this decides how buildings experience a quake.

- **P-waves** vibrate **parallel** to the direction of the wave. They exert pressure on the material, creating alternating zones of **compression and rarefaction** (density differences). A house feels them as a sudden jolt or thump.
- **S-waves** vibrate **perpendicular** to the direction of travel, in the vertical plane. They create **troughs and crests** in the material they pass through. Their sideways shaking is far more harmful to structures than the P-wave jolt.
- **Surface waves** are the last to arrive. Some make the ground roll like ocean swells; others shake it side to side horizontally. Because they stay near the surface and carry large amplitude, they cause most damage. (Seismologists call the two main kinds Love waves and Rayleigh waves.)

**Reading a seismogram.** A seismograph's trace stays nearly flat until the **P-waves** arrive with small wiggles; then the **S-waves** arrive with bigger ones; then the large **surface waves**. The **time gap between P and S arrivals** grows with distance from the epicentre — like the gap between seeing lightning and hearing thunder. With the S–P gap from **three stations**, scientists draw three circles on a map; where they meet is the epicentre (triangulation).

This gap is also why **early warning** is possible: P-waves travel at about 6 km/s in the crust and S-waves at about 3.5 km/s, so a city 100 km away gets several seconds' warning before the damaging shaking.

sections.h: Shadow zones: the clue to a liquid core
sections.md:
Here is the cleverest part. Earthquake waves are recorded at seismographs far away. Scientists noticed that there are areas on the Earth where certain waves are **not recorded at all**. These are **shadow zones**.

- Seismographs located within **105°** of the epicentre recorded both P and S waves.
- Seismographs beyond **145°** from the epicentre recorded only P-waves, not S-waves.
- A zone **between 105° and 145°** from the epicentre recorded **neither** P nor S waves directly. This is the **shadow zone for P-waves**.
- The **shadow zone for S-waves** is much larger: it covers everything **beyond 105°** — a little more than 40 per cent of the Earth's surface.

Why? S-waves vanish beyond 105° because they cannot pass through the **outer core**, which must therefore be **liquid**. P-waves pass through the core, but are **refracted** (bent) sharply at the core boundary, leaving a ring between 105° and 145° where they do not arrive.

Every earthquake has its own shadow zone, centred opposite its epicentre. By putting together data from thousands of earthquakes, seismologists mapped the core boundary at a depth of about **2,900 km**.

This was the work of scientists such as **Beno Gutenberg** (who located the core–mantle boundary in 1914) and **Inge Lehmann** (who discovered in 1936 that there is a solid inner core within the liquid outer core).
